stem: A pregnant client taking sertraline asks why the newborn may need observation after third-trimester exposure. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.A: Some exposed newborns have developed findings such as respiratory distress, feeding difficulty, tremor, or jitteriness
options.B: Every exposed newborn will require prolonged intensive-care hospitalization
options.C: Sertraline exposure in late pregnancy has no reported neonatal effects
options.D: The only expected neonatal effect is a congenital limb deformity appearing at birth

rationale: Current sertraline labeling reports that neonates exposed to sertraline and other SSRIs/SNRIs late in the third trimester have developed complications including respiratory distress, feeding difficulty, tremor, and jitteriness. The label directs clinicians to monitor third-trimester-exposed neonates for persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn and drug discontinuation syndrome. These complications are possible, not inevitable, so B is an unsupported absolute.
educational_objective: Teach that late-pregnancy sertraline exposure can be associated with neonatal respiratory, feeding, and neurologic adaptation symptoms and warrants newborn monitoring without implying that every exposed infant will be severely affected.
source_organization: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed

source_claim_supported: Late third-trimester exposure to sertraline can be associated with neonatal respiratory distress, feeding difficulty, tremor, jitteriness and other complications; monitoring is advised.

correction_summary: Changed the vague SSRI-class question to a sertraline-specific third-trimester item anchored to the current label. Removed the non-label shorthand 'poor neonatal adaptation syndrome' and the implication that NICU admission is either expected or impossible.
audit_findings: A is directly supported by the sertraline label. B is an unsupported universal outcome, C contradicts documented postmarketing reports, and D invents a specific congenital-effect pattern not supported by the cited section. No second-answer ambiguity, cueing, or unsupported precision remains.
